analysis.one_liner: Delays the rule cutting federal student aid from career programs whose graduates can't repay their loans.
analysis.headline: Six Republican senators sponsored the bill, but it never received a hearing or vote; it died in committee when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped the Education Department from finalizing its "gainful employment" rule, which cuts federal student aid from career training programs whose graduates don't earn enough to repay their loans. It required the Department to first publish a full analysis of the rule's impact on every type of college and student group — including Pell Grant recipients, minority students, and veterans — wait 90 days, and have the Government Accountability Office check that analysis for accuracy before any final rule could take effect. The bill was referred to the Senate education committee on the day it was introduced and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the bill would have benefited for-profit career colleges, which draw large amounts of federal student aid into programs the proposed rule would penalize. A mandatory 90-day waiting period plus a GAO review would have delayed any aid cutoff, keeping federal loan and grant dollars flowing to programs with poor job and debt outcomes.

how_it_helps.text: The bill barred the Education Department from issuing or implementing any final gainful employment rule — including the one proposed in March 2014 — until 90 days after it published a complete data analysis of the rule's impact on all postsecondary programs and students, and until the Comptroller General reviewed that analysis for accuracy and completeness.

Because the proposed rule would cut title IV federal student aid (Pell Grants and federal loans) from career programs whose graduates' debt is high relative to their earnings, delaying it would preserve that aid revenue for the colleges that rely on it.

analysis.who_pays: If passed, students and taxpayers would bear the cost: borrowers — including veterans and minority students — would keep taking on federal debt for career programs that don't lead to jobs paying enough to repay it, and taxpayers would keep funding Pell Grants and loans for those programs while the delay ran.

drawbacks.text: The delay would have left students enrolled in low-performing career programs eligible for federal loans and grants longer, meaning more graduates carrying debt for training that did not pay off — the exact problem the proposed rule was designed to catch.

The bill singled out one specific rulemaking for an extraordinary set of procedural hurdles — a mandatory full data analysis, a fixed 90-day waiting period, and a GAO accuracy review — a delay tactic that could have pushed the rule past the end of the administration's term.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill framed its delay as a transparency safeguard, and analyzing a rule's impact on students is a legitimate request. But the practical effect was to postpone a consumer protection that would cut federal money from career programs whose graduates can't repay their loans, and the added analysis and review steps were designed to slow the rule down, not to make it fairer. The cost fell on students and taxpayers; the benefit fell on the colleges.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent the bill to its Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced; the committee never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Flake introduced the bill on September 18, 2014, with five Republican cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
No further action was ever taken: the bill received no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and expired at the end of the 113th Congress on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Students and taxpayers came out ahead, because the delay never became law and the Department's process for cutting aid to low-performing career programs was left free to move forward.

for.name: Jeff Flake
for.role: U.S. Senator from Arizona; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require a data analysis and 90-day delay before any final gainful employment rule could take effect.

for.name: 5 of 45 Senate Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors (McCain, Hatch, Isakson, and two others)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill when it was introduced.

for.name: For-profit college industry
for.role: Sector facing the proposed gainful employment rule
for.what_they_did: Ran a well-documented lobbying and public campaign against the gainful employment rule, of which this bill was one legislative vehicle.

against.name: Tom Harkin
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it to die in committee at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors were Senate Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and the Democratic-controlled committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The gainful employment rule would cut federal Pell Grant and loan eligibility from career programs whose graduates' debt exceeds a set share of their earnings — programs concentrated in the for-profit sector. Delaying the rule preserves those federal aid dollars for the colleges, while students at weak programs keep borrowing for training that doesn't pay off.

The bill required the Department to analyze the rule's impact on all categories of institutions, since some public and nonprofit schools also offer career programs that could be caught by the rule. Most of the rule's penalties were expected to fall on for-profit schools, so the effect here is minor.
